https://www.politico.eu/article/german-f.text: BERLIN — German officials must do more to convince voters of continued support for Ukraine and the country’s commitments to NATO, Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul said Thursday. NATO is undergoing a “political stress test” both from the external threat posed by Russia and from skepticism at home that had become “visible and tangible” in recent state elections, he said at the conference of German ambassadors in Berlin. He made a similar appeal over Ukraine, saying Germany would continue to stand by Kyiv and arguing that its support was not only for Ukraine but “for the benefit of our security in Europe.” Advertisement Advertisement The call comes after the AfD won 43.8% in the regional election in Saxony-Anhalt, more than doubling its 2021 result and leaving Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s Christian Democrats a distant second at 17.2 %. Wadephul argued Thursday that the way forward was not to retreat from Germany’s commitments, but to do a better job of explaining why they matter. He cast the challenge in stark historical terms, invoking the collapse of Germany’s democracy between the two World Wars. “Germany knows from the Weimar Republic what could happen if Democrats are not ready to defend their system,” he said. “We have to show that we have learned our lesson.” The Weimar Republic, Germany’s first parliamentary democracy, was progressively hollowed out amid economic crisis, political paralysis and growing support for anti-democratic forces before Adolf Hitler was appointed chancellor in 1933. As for the results of Sunday's vote, they were not only the AfD’s strongest-ever showing, but the highest vote share won by any party in the state since German reunification. During the campaign, AfD lead candidate Ulrich Siegmund repeatedly presented spending abroad as money missing at home. He told regional broadcaster MDR that Germany was “giving away money all over the world” and pointed specifically to support for Kyiv: “Every minute, €20,000 goes to Ukraine. That is all money we are missing.” Advertisement Advertisement That message is feeding into an increasingly uncomfortable guns-versus-butter debate in Berlin, just as Merz’s coalition negotiates the 2027 budget. Germany is set to spend roughly €140 billion on defense next year while facing mounting pressure over pensions, health care and other public services. The scale of the shift is stark: Defense spending next year will almost match the roughly €145 billion federal contribution to the pension system, according to Kiel Institute calculations. In 2022, Germany spent about €50 billion on defense compared with €115 billion on pensions. NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte backed Wadephul’s broader message, telling the ambassadors that Germany’s choices had consequences far beyond its borders. “I count on every one of you in this room to carry that message with you: that a stronger Germany makes Europe stronger, that a stronger Europe makes NATO stronger,” he said, speaking at the same conference. Rutte also played down the risk that electoral gains by far-right parties could weaken the alliance. NATO would work with “whoever is elected,” he said, adding that he had “no doubt that the alliance will stay very strong.”

Prefer Newsweek on Google to see more of our trusted coverage when you search. Only nine nations in the world are known to possess their own nuclear weapons programs, three of which—the United States, the United Kingdom and France—are members of the NATO alliance. But five more NATO states host U.S. nuclear weapons on their soil in line with the bloc's nuclear sharing program, an arrangement developed in the 1950s in a bid to counter the Soviet Union's conventional military superiority in Europe in the event that the Cold War erupted into full-scale conflict. Today, these countries include Belgium, Germany, Italy, the Netherlands and Turkey. Each maintains a stockpile of B61 gravity bombs that can be fitted to a variety of aircraft deployed among NATO members, including variants of the F-15, F-16 and F-35 fighter aircraft, as well as the European Panavia Tornado. Read More on World And as European nations once again worry about potential escalation from Moscow as the Russia -Ukraine war enters a dangerous new phase, another NATO member, Poland , has entered into a fierce debate over whether or not to bring U.S. weapons of mass destruction onto its territory. Following a meeting with Elbridge Colby, U.S. under secretary of defense for policy, on Thursday, Polish Deputy Defense Minister Pawel Zalewski was asked by reporters if Warsaw would seek to join the NATO nuclear sharing program. He responded, "No. I would like to say this very clearly and openly: Poland does not want nuclear warheads on its territory." The comments, however, prompted a wave of criticism from figures aligned with President Karol Nawrocki, who leads the right-wing populist Law and Justice opposition party. On Friday, Nawrocki's International Policy Bureau chief, Marcin Przydacz, slammed Zalewski's remarks as "bizarre, absurd and completely inconsistent with what Poland has been saying so far and what the policy of the Polish state is." "Poland also wants to have the presence of warheads on its territory," Przydacz said. "Today, there is no such infrastructure, but if we join the [nuclear-sharing] program, such infrastructure will have to be built." Why Poland? Why Now? Long overshadowed by traditional European powers such as France, Germany and the U.K., Poland has increasingly emerged as a military leader on the continent since becoming the first country to break with the communist Eastern Bloc in 1989, two years before the fall of the Soviet Union. Poland now commands the third-largest army in NATO, behind only the U.S. and Turkey. It also devotes the largest share of its GDP to defense among allies, at 4.3 percent. But Warsaw's impressive build-up has not left it immune to the spillover effects of the war in Ukraine, which Poland borders directly, along with Russia's Kaliningrad exclave and Moscow's ally, Belarus. Drones and missiles have crossed into Polish territory on several occasions since the beginning of the conflict in February 2022, most notably an incident last September in which Russia was blamed for the incursion of 19 drones onto Polish territory. This year may prove even more precarious for Poland as the Kremlin looks to increase the pressure on NATO to counter slowing gains in Ukraine and Kyiv's costly campaign of long-range attacks against Russian gas infrastructure. Reports that Moscow may be planning to escalate in the form of a new mobilization or even operations on NATO soil were further fueled by a surprise visit by the CIA chief to the Russian capital earlier this week. While Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov dismissed such speculation on Thursday as having "no basis in reality," officials in Warsaw remain on high alert. Foreign Minister and Deputy Prime Minister Radek Sikorski warned last month that Russia may pursue a "false flag operation" to justify direct action against a NATO member. Related Story What a Russian Attack on NATO Could Look Like As CIA Trip Fuels Speculation Some analysts argue the presence of U.S. nuclear weapons on Polish territory may fortify deterrence in light of growing tensions. "Involving Poland in nuclear sharing would help convince Russia that the U.S. and NATO are seriously thinking about responding with nuclear weapons to nuclear attack on the Alliance’s eastern flank," Artur Kacprzyk, an analyst at the Polish Institute of International Affairs ' International Security Program, told Newsweek . He argued that NATO's nuclear-sharing program's message of unity was undermined by the fact that no nations along the alliance's eastern flank directly across from Russia participated. Poland, in particular, he said, was "firmly in the crosshairs" of Russian Iskander short-range ballistic missile systems deployed to Kaliningrad and Belarus. "Deploying nuclear weapons in Poland would be a particularly strong political signal from the U.S. and NATO, while also offering additional options for using U.S. nuclear bombs in Europe," Kacprzyk said. "When stationed closer to Russia they could be to strike deeper and faster, with lesser warning time for Russian air defense." ... At What Cost? Among the primary reasons that Kacprzyk argued nuclear deterrence remained relevant even in an age of hybrid warfare tactics increasingly being attributed to Moscow was that "Russia relies on nuclear weapons as a cover for aggression," and has only "doubled down on nuclear intimidation" since the beginning of the war in Ukraine. Yet the public rift that has recently emerged among senior Polish officials indicates a lack of consensus on how far the nation was willing to go to shore up its defense. Lukasz Kulesa, deputy head of research at the Polish Institute of International Affairs, acknowledged that Poland's full entry into the NATO nuclear-sharing pact would inevitably have consequences. "Of course, Russia would criticize such a move and present it as 'proof' of U.S. and NATO’s aggressive intensions," Kulesa told Newsweek . "Internally at NATO, some members states may question whether such forward deployment would not be too escalatory towards Russia, and whether it would be operationally justified," Kulesa said. "After all, it would bring U.S. nuclear weapons within the range of more Russian missiles." That only five of the alliance's non-nuclear member states participate in the nuclear sharing arrangement speaks to its complexity. Canada and Greece previously participated but withdrew, while Denmark and Norway have explicitly opposed the deployment of nuclear weapons on their soil. Spain's 1982 entry into NATO prohibits nuclear weapons from being hosted on its territory, and France, which has its own arsenal, is the only NATO member that does not participate in the alliance's broader nuclear planning group. Given the controversy surrounding the decision, a "less ambitious" and "less risky" option Kulesa identified would "involve certifying Polish F-35s and pilots for the nuclear mission but without the actual deployment on Polish soil," thus potentially constituting "a good compromise at this point." But despite the debate playing out in Warsaw, he saw "broad support in Poland among the main political parties for joining 'directly' NATO’s nuclear mission." "The question seems to be more about what’s feasible at this point—most importantly, what the Trump administration is willing to offer or agree to." http://www.europesun.com/news/279367226/.text: EU anti-'disinfo' effort falls apart after trying to be honest about the US RT.com 12 Oct 2026, 00:17 GMT+10 When one panel dared name Washington, Brussels and its allies fled - because it has always been about power, not truth It was supposed to be a safe space for all the Karens and institutionally-backed wine moms who spend their days policing public discourse like it's neighborhood Block Watch fodder. Instead, this year's EU #Disinfo2026 confab in Lithuania turned into a bust. What happened was basically the equivalent of a friend's husband getting called out ahead of the confab as the neighborhood perv, prompting everyone to ghost the meetup at the last minute. The problem? A scheduled panel called 'USA as a FIMI threat: adapt, acknowledge, push back.' Incidentally, 'FIMI threat' is one of those hip acronyms that these people are overpaid to come up with so that it sounds like they're doing something only those with their rare expertise can wrangle. In reality, it just means 'foreign information manipulation and interference,' and the average seventh grader can push back against it on social media if they want to. Usually with memes that are a lot more savvy, and without billing taxpayers. The meetup was organized by the Brussels-backed EU Disinfo Lab, and was apparently such a great use of EU funds that the bloc had its own sponsorship logo taken right off the promotional signage and bailed on itself. "The organizers chose to frame some of the discussions in a way which does not align with the positions held by the EU," said EU foreign affairs spokesman Christian Wigand. And Lithuania couldn't even be bothered to roll down the street in their pajamas to attend this thing. "Lithuania has cancelled its participation in Disinfo 2026 as several parts of the conference program differ from the official position of the government," its Foreign Ministry said . Color me shocked that people who put an extraordinary amount of effort into corralling the masses into establishment-approved groupthink have just had a collective anaphylactic reaction to a deviation from it. What about Canada? Surely it maintained its presence, right? Particularly since there's a lot of talk in Canada these days about entities close to Trump, including State Department officials, getting involved in manipulation efforts to gin up incredibly long-shot independence movements in the provinces of Alberta and Quebec , with a view to gaining control of Canadian resources and then pressuring the federal government into doing what Trump wants. So you'd think that Canada would have relished the opportunity to head over to this conference and confront Washington, knowing that its behavior would be a focus. At the very least, it would have been a chance to demonstrate that all this talk about defending democracy and information integrity extends beyond smack talking from a comfortable distance. "Following changes to the framing of several panel discussions, Global Affairs Canada decided to revise its participation in those sessions at the EU DisinfoLab 2026 conference," a Canadian government spokeswoman said . What could possibly have been behind all these US allies bailing in such a coordinated fashion? Couldn't have been because they were all being pressured, right? Surely, nobody would ever think of manipulating anyone into not attending a conference about manipulation. "While we are unable to comment on the details of diplomatic conversations, it should not be a surprise that countries would disaffiliate from this conference upon learning that it labeled the US a 'FIMI threat,'" the State Department said . "Labeling the United States a 'FIMI threat' - a term normally reserved for describing influence operations of adversaries - undermines shared goals and should alarm those involved." Thanks for confirming that "disinfo" can only ever come from entities that you don't like and depends on the source rather than a critical assessment of the info itself. To be fair, it's worth defining terms. "Disinformation" seems to be a convenient catch-all phrase used by the Western establishment to marginalize a wide range of discourse - from adverse opinions that contradict the establishment's own mass mind-bending efforts, to straight-up nonsense. The fact that they don't make enough of a distinction between those two things is to their discredit. There's a rather significant difference between someone challenging an official narrative and someone insisting that the planet is run by a cabal of lizard people. But both have become fodder for the same sprawling industry of experts and other taxpayer-funded initiatives. Before the internet and social media, the average person didn't need some Western apparatchik to tell them that the guy ranting on the street corner was a nutjob. Or to know that states have a tendency to spin in their own self-interest. Or to take whatever you hear around the water cooler at work with a grain of salt. But apparently, now that we're all connected online, everyone's brains have gone to mush and we need self-appointed babysitters to tell us what to think under the pretext of protecting us. And certainly not just protecting their power, surely. The public, once trusted to exercise a modicum of judgment, has been demoted to a classroom of toddlers who would eat the crayons the minute they're unsupervised. Washington's spin didn't start with Trump. It's just that it's now so glaring that not even America's friends can play along with it. Like his framing of the current French leftist riots as being caused by migrants and Islamists, despite French intelligence plainly stating that it's the annual leftist activist effort. But hey, it suits Israel's routine framing of everything in every country as being about Islam, which seems to be a big objective of Trump these days - keeping Israel and his Israeli donors like Miriam Adelson and Republican Israeli-backed think tanks happy. See what I did there? Countered some info with other info. Not hard, right? And all without adult supervision. Unlike some folks who have made a career out of demanding that everyone else show their work, and clearly aren't especially keen on having to ask the same of Trump's America. But instead of showing up to their own conference and accepting the obvious - that Trump contradicts himself every five minutes all day long - it turns out that some of these guardians of information integrity ultimately decided that the cause wasn't so critical to democracy that it was worth a Trump-grade headache. Guess it's a lot easier to keep lecturing the powerless than risk inconveniencing the powerful. What a stunning profile in courage from our fearless Western leaders. One might even call it a double standard. Although perhaps they should convene a panel before deciding, lest it qualify as disinfo. https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cmly.text: Figure caption, "We're going to fight" - How a paper mill's uncertain future could devastate tiny Quebec town By Jessica Murphy ,Â Canada digital editor Â and Â Nadine Yousif ,Â Senior Canada reporter Published 57 minutes ago As you cross the Ottawa river into TÃ©miscaming, Quebec, the paper mill takes up much of the horizon. The town itself was built over a century ago, around the mill and the region's forests filled with pine, birch, spruce and fir. Now, the main employer and economic anchor sits idle after trade talks broke down between Canada and the US and President Donald Trump imposed more tariffs on the country. Most of the millâs 360 employees are out of work, kept afloat for the moment with partial pay from government tariff-relief. For some, like Nadine Suley, the shuttering of the mill could mark not just a lost livelihood, but a lost way of life. She is not "a city girl", and is heading out moose hunting later to take advantage of the short season, like much of the town. She quips they'll all need the free meat provided by the animals this year. "It's not just a job. It's our home," Suley says, adding that the US tariffs on her town feel like "a personal attack". In early October, American owner RYAM went ahead with an "economic shutdown" of the mill for "an indefinite period". Property values in TÃ©miscaming fell almost overnight, and "For Sale" signs dot the yards of modest middle-class homes that make up most of the town. There are fears that essential service people - from grocery store clerks to the doctors at the small local hospital - could also be on their way out. "If the mill goes down, it'll turn into a ghost town," says Ronnie Raymond, who like many in the town comes from a family of mill workers. "There'll be nothing, nothing left. There's no work for anybody, really. It's scary." Image source, BBC/Jessica Murphy Image caption, The paper mill has served as the economic engine of TÃ©miscaming for over a century. At a high level, Canada's economy has weathered the ongoing trade war with the US, its largest customer. The national unemployment rate has remained largely steady at around 6.5% since Trump's tariffs were first implemented. It's been coupled with tepid but consistent economic growth. But a closer look at the numbers shows pockets of deep pain in industries directly hit by US tariffs of up to 50%, like steel, aluminium, automobiles and - in the case of TÃ©miscaming - lumber, pulp and paper. It raises questions about whether the Carney government is doing enough to help those struggling while a trade deal remains elusive. "If there was 10% of job loss in Toronto or Montreal or Quebec City or Vancouver, it'd be all over the news, and it'd be a lot of pressure on the governments to do something,â says StÃ©phane Lefebvre, an employee and union leader, whose father and grandfather also worked at the mill. What tariffs has Trump introduced and why? Published 22 August White House lifts tariffs on some Canadian goods as midterm elections loom Published 7 days ago That economic pain could have ripple effects on the entire forestry industry in the region, including saw mills and trucking. One local contractor told the BBC he has already had to lay off 13 people. The last time the town faced a threat this existential was in 1973, when the mill's then-American owner threatened to shut it down, prompting the local workers and managers to come together and purchase it. They turned it into Tembec, a Quebec-owned, international company with branches across North America and France. The workers now hope to do it again, mobilising a coalition of locals who want to buy the plant back from RYAM, which purchased it in 2017. "We're hoping that lightning will hit twice," Lefebvre says, speaking inside the town's union hall. But he contends that they cannot do so without significant help from Prime Minister Mark Carney and the Quebec government, either in the form of tariff relief or financial support. Suley notes that the prime minister has placed emphasis on "buy local" and supporting Canadian workers since he was elected. Backing the town's bid to buy back the mill, she says, would be a way for Carney to fulfil that pledge. In an email to the BBC, RYAM said it would not comment on a potential sale of the plant or any prospective buyers. Image source, BBC/Nadine Yousif Image caption, StÃ©phane Lefebvre, his father and grandfather all worked at the paper mill in TÃ©miscaming. Mayor Alain Gauthier doesn't blame RYAM for its decision. He calls US tariffs "a bomb to shut down our manufacturing in Canada". He wants Ottawa to retaliate with its own duties on the board products coming into Canada from the US, currently tariff-free. And he says that while politicians have said Canada is in an economic war with the US, "in reality we see absolutely no evidence of war measures being taken". "We feel we got into a war with kid's water guns to fight back." Some, like Lefebvre, feel that forestry has taken a back seat in the fight to save other tariffed industries like steel and autos. This month, Industry Minister MÃ©lanie Joly threatened Stelco - one of Canada's largest steelmakers - with financial penalties or a forced asset sale should they go ahead with the planned layoffs of some 500 workers due to steel tariffs pressure. Stelco in Hamilton, near Toronto, is owned by US-based Cleveland-Cliffs, which committed to keeping jobs in Canada when it bought the firm in 2024. Last week, Carney and Ontario Premier Doug Ford announced nearly C$9bn ($6.4bn; Â£4.8bn) to help Ontario's steel and auto sector. The funds will be used to help the industries modernise, strengthen domestic demand and open new markets overseas, they said. SÃ©bastien Lemire, the elected MP for TÃ©miscaming from the Bloc QuÃ©bÃ©cois party, told the BBC that he is "very concerned and worried" about what he calls inaction from the Carney government to support the town and Quebec's forestry industry more broadly. A spokesperson for Minister Joly told the BBC in a statement that the government has made available $400m to support the forestry sector in rural and remote areas. It has also launched a programme to help businesses impacted by tariffs to access cash-flow while they work to pivot away from US markets. On the TÃ©miscaming mill, the spokesperson said that the government "is actively working with all parties involved to find a viable solution to the issues facing the company, while responsibly managing Canadians' dollars." Image source, Supplied/StÃ©phane Lefebvre Image caption, TÃ©miscaming residents gathered for a Union-led rally to support the mill's workers and draw attention to the woes of the lumber industry. In August, after the breakdown in trade talks, the US imposed 50% duties on a some C$28bn of Canadian goods, including wood and paper products like pulp, stationery and boxes. Canada in response imposed its own "dollar-for-dollar" counter-tariffs. The TÃ©miscaming mill, which produces paperboard used in frozen-food packaging across North America and in the scratch-off lottery tickets commonly found at convenience stores, sends roughly 75% of its production to the US. Trump argues these import taxes boost US manufacturing and create jobs - essentially seeking to protect US workers who could face similar fates to those in TÃ©miscaming. Frank Dottori has been through all of this before. Now in his 80s and retired in TÃ©miscaming, he was an engineer at the mill that was instrumental in organising its employees in the 1970s to take a 10% cut in order to collectively purchase it. He went on to become CEO. Their ambitions were seen as foolish at the time, and he recalls being "politely ejected" by the Quebec premier when he first came knocking for support. But they prevailed with the help of the labour union and an ex-employee with executive experience and plenty of swagger. Dottori attributes their success to this person's forceful charisma. Dottori said the new generation of workers need someone just as bold. "Does the local group have that? Highly unlikely. Can they get it? Yeah, if they if they organise themselves," he said. Image source, BBC/Nadine Yousif Image caption, Frank Dottori led the effort to buy the TÃ©miscaming mill in the 1970s during a period of economic hardship It is also imperative, he says, that US tariffs be lifted to restore the mill's long-term economic viability, at least in the short term. Many workers in TÃ©miscaming say they are placing some hope in the upcoming US midterm elections to put pressure on Trump â whose approval ratings have fallen among Americans, according to polls â to ease some of his tariffs on Canada. "We'll take any help we can get," Suley says, adding: "There are Americans that care what's going on, and it's affecting them too." There are signs the Trump administration is taking note of that pressure, with some tariffs on Canadian goods lifted last week after lobbying from Republican Maine Senator Susan Collins, who is running for re-election in November. Those changes don't apply to products made at TÃ©miscaming's mill, however. Suley and others hope a resolution will come quickly, before winter, when sub-zero temperatures could freeze equipment at the idle plant, causing damage that would make reopening even more difficult. In the meantime, Lefebvre says he is committed to making the dream of local ownership of the mill a reality, regardless of what happens. "We're in Game Seven right now," he says. "We're gonna play till the last whistle."
